---
title: "decision trees"
---

## intuition

- a decision tree recursively splits the data by asking yes/no questions about features, aiming to make each resulting group as "pure" as possible
- geometrically, a tree draws axis-aligned regions in feature space — every split is a horizontal or vertical cut on one feature; predictions are constant within each resulting region
- the algorithm is greedy: at each node it picks the single best split given everything split so far, and never revisits that choice — fast to fit, but not guaranteed to find the globally optimal tree

## choosing a split

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| | regression | classification |
|---|---|---|
| predicts | a number | a class |
| leaf value | mean of $y$ in the region | majority class in the region |
| split criterion | variance (mse) reduction | gini impurity or entropy reduction |

:::

- **classification**: gini impurity at a node with $k$ classes is $\text{gini}=1-\sum_k p_k^2$, where $p_k$ is the fraction of samples in class $k$ — a pure node (one class only) has gini $=0$. entropy is $h=-\sum_k p_k\log_2 p_k$. information gain is the parent's impurity minus the weighted average impurity of the children; the split chosen is whichever maximises information gain
- **regression**: a split is scored by how much it reduces variance (mse) within the resulting children compared to the parent — the chosen split maximises that reduction
- at each node, every feature and candidate threshold is tried, the criterion computed, and the best one kept — this is roughly $O(n\cdot p\cdot\log n)$ per level, which gets expensive on wide or very large data

## stopping criteria

- common stopping rules: a maximum depth, a minimum number of samples per leaf, a minimum information gain to justify a split, or simply splitting until every leaf is pure
- without a stopping rule, a tree keeps splitting until every leaf holds a single point — a textbook case of [overfitting / high variance](../training-evaluation/bias-variance.qmd#recognising-underfitting--overfitting): perfect training accuracy, unstable predictions on new data

## practical considerations

- a single tree is intuitive and interpretable — every prediction can be read off as a sequence of yes/no questions — but it's brittle: small changes in the training data can produce a noticeably different tree (high variance). this is exactly what [random forests](random-forests.qmd) and [gradient boosting](gradient-boosting.qmd) are built to fix, by combining many trees rather than relying on one
- trees split on raw feature values and thresholds, so monotonic transforms (scaling, log transforms) don't change the resulting splits — consistent with tree-based models being scale-insensitive, see [data type drives preprocessing choices](../training-evaluation/feature-engineering.qmd#data-type-drives-preprocessing-choices)
- trees capture non-linear relationships and feature interactions automatically, without the manual feature engineering (polynomial terms, interaction terms) that [linear](../supervised-learning/linear-regression.qmd) or [logistic](../supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) regression would need to do the same
